Abstract
Background  Insulin resistance (IR) is an established independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD). 
Although numerous simple surrogate indicators for IR have been proposed, their comparative predictive utility for 
CVD remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the associations between nine IR surrogate indicators and incident 
CVD and to comparatively assess their predictive capacities using nationally representative data from China.
Methods  7,662 participants without CVD from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) 
were included in the study. Nine IR surrogate measures including triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, triglyceride to 
high-density lipoprotein ratio (TG/HDL), metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR), Chinese visceral adiposity 
index (CVAI), lipid accumulation product (LAP), atherogenic index of plasma (AIP), triglyceride glucose-body mass 
index (TyG-BMI), triglyceride glucose-waist circumference (TyG-WC), and triglyceride glucose-waist-to-height ratio 
(TyG-WHtR) were calculated. Cox model and restricted cubic spline model were used to estimate the relationships 
between distinct IR surrogates and incident CVD. We also computed the time-dependent Harrell’s concordance index 
(C-index) to compare the predictive performance of IR surrogates.
Results  After a mean follow-up duration of 8.2 years, a total of 1,906 individuals developed CVD. The full adjusted 
cox model revealed that per SD increase in all IR indicators was significantly associated with elevated CVD risk, with 
the hazard ratio (95%CI) of 1.09 (1.04–1.14) for TyG; 1.05 (1.01–1.10) for TG/HDL-C; 1.09 (1.03–1.14) for METS-IR; 1.13 
(1.08–1.19) for CVAI; 1.07 (1.03–1.12) for LAP; 1.08 (1.03–1.13) for AIP; 1.10 (1.05–1.15) for TyG-BMI; 1.11 (1.06–1.16) for 
TyG-WC; and 1.11 (1.05–1.16) for TyG-WHtR. Predictive performance analysis showed TyG had the highest C-index of 
0.742 (95% CI, 0.737–0.747).
Conclusions  Among nine IR surrogates, the TyG index exhibited the highest predictive performance for incident 
CVD in Chinese middle-aged and older adults. Acknowledging limitations such as the observational design and self-
reported outcomes, our findings support the TyG index as a simple, powerful, and clinically accessible tool for early 
CVD risk prediction.

Introduction
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause 
of global mortality, imposing substantial health and 
economic burdens worldwide [1, 2]. Data from Global 
Burden of Disease Study [3] has indicated that the age-
standardized incidence rate of CVD in Chinese popu­
lation continuously increased from 1990 to 2019. It is 
estimated that 330  million people in China currently 
have CVD. In China, CVD has become the primary cause 
of mortality, with approximately 5.09  million Chinese 
deaths were attributed to it in 2021 [4]. Recent research 
indicated a persistent upward trajectory in CVD inci­
dence and CVD-related mortality rates through 2030 
in China [5]. Insulin resistance (IR), characterized by 
reduced insulin sensitivity, impaired glucose utilization, 
and disordered lipid metabolism [6, 7], has been identi­
fied as an independent risk factor for many chronic dis­
eases such as atherosclerotic CVD [8–11] and cancer [12, 
13], and this association was observed in both diabetic 
and non-diabetic patients. However, the gold standard 
for IR assessment—the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic 
clamp—is invasive and expensive. This critical limitation 
underscores the urgent need to establish accessible and 
reliable surrogate indicators of IR for effective CVD risk 
stratification.
In recent years, numerous studies have proposed sim­
ple and practical surrogate indicators for IR, including 
the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index [14], triglyceride to 
high-density lipoprotein ratio (TG/HDL) [15], metabolic 
score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) [16], Chinese vis­
ceral adiposity index (CVAI) [17], lipid accumulation 
product (LAP) [18], atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) 
[19], triglyceride glucose-body mass index (TyG-BMI) 
[20], triglyceride glucose-waist circumference (TyG-WC) 
[21], and triglyceride glucose-waist-to-height ratio (TyG-
WHtR) [22]. These metrics, derived from routine meta­
bolic parameters (e.g., fasting glucose, lipid profiles, and 
anthropometric measurements), are recognized as reli­
able tools for assessing IR and demonstrate associations 
with CVD incidence and mortality. However, no prior 
study has systematically compared the predictive capaci­
ties of these indicators for cardiovascular events within 
a single, large-scale cohort, limiting their clinical util­
ity. Comparing the predictive ability of different IR sur­
rogates for CVD in a large-scale prospective cohort and 
identifying the optimal indicator would enable clinicians 
to diagnose IR early using routine, low-cost biochemi­
cal tests. This is crucial for achieving early diagnosis 
and intervention of CVD and reducing the overall CVD 
burden.
Therefore, considering the large number of CVD 
patients in China, this study aims to evaluate the asso­
ciations between nine IR surrogates and incident CVD, 
while comparatively assessing their predictive capacity, 
using nationally representative data from the China 
Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS).
Methods
Study population
The China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study 
(CHARLS) is a longitudinal study of individuals over age 
45 in China, which was designed to better understand 
the socioeconomic determinants and consequences of 
aging. A total of 17,705 individuals 45 and older from 28 
provinces (150 counties /districts) of China were selected 
using multistage stratified probability proportional-to-
size sampling strategy [23, 24] as representative samples 
at baseline. Follow-up surveys were later carried out in 
2013, 2015, 2018, and 2020, with the most recent data 
now accessible for download on the website. ​(​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​c​h​
a​r​l​s​.​p​k​u​.​e​d​u​.​c​n​/​)​.​
The data analyzed in the present study was based on 
CHARLS data from 2011 to 2020. Of the initial 25,586 
participants, we first excluded those who only completed 
one survey (n = 2,118) and those with missing baseline 
information on CVD or cancer history (n = 3,784). And 
then, we further excluded participants with prevalent 
CVD at baseline (n = 2,627) and those with missing TG, 
FPG, HDL-C, or the other necessary anthropometric 
measurements (n = 9,149). Finally, among the remain­
ing participants, we excluded those aged younger than 
45 years (n = 246), resulting in a final analytical cohort 
of 7,662 participants. The detailed participant selection 
process is illustrated in Fig.  1. To assess for potential 
selection bias, we compared the baseline characteristics 
of the included participants with those excluded (Supple­
mentary Table 1 in Additional file 1). The CHARLS has 
been approved by Institutional Review Board of Peking 
University (IRB00001052-11015), and all participants 
have signed an informed consent form before the entire 
experiment.
Assessment of covariates and IR surrogate measures
Socio-demographic information including age, sex, edu­
cation, marital status, residence and health behaviors 
information including smoking and drinking status, 
were collected by face-to-face interview using a standard 
questionnaire. Anthropometric measurements such as 
height, weight, and waist circumference (WC) were mea­
sured according to uniform standards. Overnight fasting 
venous blood was only collected at baseline (2011) and 
wave 3 (2015). The bioassays of blood samples were per­
formed at the Youanmen Center for Clinical Laboratory 
of Capital Medical University. In this study, we defined 
smoke status as “never smoking”, “former smoker” and 
“current smoker” according the questionnaire. Educa­
tion level was grouped as “less than lower secondary 
education”, “upper secondary & vocational training”

Assessment of outcome
The primary outcome in this study was the incidence of 
CVD, which was a composite outcome comprising heart 
disease (heart attack, coronary heart disease, angina, 
congestive heart failure, other heart problems) and 
stroke. The outcome was defined based on the inquiries 
concerning CVD: “Have you been diagnosed with heart 
attack, coronary heart disease, angina, congestive heart 
failure, or other heart problems?” and “Have you been 
diagnosed with stroke?”. Participants were defined as 
having incident CVD if they reported no heart disease 
or stroke at baseline but developed these conditions dur­
ing follow-up. All the above questions were obtained by 
professional investigators who received uniform training 
through face-to-face interviews.
Statistical analyses
Continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard 
deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range), while cat­
egorical variables were reported as numbers (percent­
age). Study participants were stratified into two groups 
(non-CVD vs. CVD) for the analysis of baseline charac­
teristic. Comparisons between groups were performed 
using t-test or Kruskal–Wallis H test for continuous vari­
ables, and chi-square tests for categorical variables. The 
comparison of baseline characteristics between groups 
was only a descriptive analysis; no multiplicity correction 
was performed.
Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression model was 
employed to investigate the association between differ­
ent IR surrogates and incidence of CVD. For each IR sur­
rogate, we either stratified it by quartiles or included it 
as a standardized continuous variable in different mod­
els. The variable selection was based on established risk 
factors for CVD identified in the previous literature [25]. 
We constructed two different models: Model 1 adjusted 
for age and sex; Model 2 further adjusted for residence, 
marriage status, education level, smoking, drinking, 
hypertension and diabetes. The association between IR 
surrogates and incidence of CVD was presented as haz­
ard ratio (HR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). The 
proportional hazards assumption was examined for each 
model using Schoenfeld residuals. A global test, as well as 
tests for individual variables, showed no significant evi­
dence of violation of this assumption (all p-values > 0.05), 
indicating that the hazard ratios were constant over time. 
Restricted cubic spline (RCS) was performed to explore 
the nonlinear relationships between different IR surro­
gates and outcome. Furthermore, subgroup analyses were 
performed using heart disease and stroke as distinct end­
points to investigate the relationships between IR surro­
gates and each outcome.
To evaluate and compare the predictive performance 
of each IR surrogate for CVD onset, time-dependent 
Harrell’s concordance index (C-index) was calculated for 
each indicator. A bootstrap-based method was employed 
to compare the differences in C-index between different 
IR surrogates. SAS version 9.4 was used for data cleaning 
and description of baseline characteristics, and all other 
analyses were performed in R version 4.4.1 (R Foundation 
for Statistical Computing). A 2-sided P < 0.05 was consid­
ered to be statistically significant.
Results
Baseline characteristic
This study included 7,662 participants with a mean 
(SD) age of 58.6 (9.2) years, of whom 4,036 (52.7%) were 
female. During a mean follow-up period of 8.2 years, inci­
dent CVD events occurred in 1,906 individuals. Results 
demonstrated neither marital status nor residence was 
significantly associated with CVD incidence (P > 0.05). 
Participants with CVD were older, had a higher pro­
portion of females, and exhibited greater prevalence of 
hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia compared with 
non-CVD participants (all P < 0.001). Metabolic profiles 
differed significantly between groups. The CVD group 
showed elevated levels of triglycerides, fasting glucose, 
BMI, waist circumference, SBP, and DBP (all P < 0.001). 
Additionally, all IR surrogate markers were significantly 
higher in the CVD group (all P < 0.001). More detailed 
information can be found in Table 1. The comparison of 
baseline characteristics between excluded and included 
participants was provided in Supplementary Table 1. 
Except for sex, drinking, smoking, and BMI, the excluded 
participants differed significantly from the included 
participants.
Relationships between IR surrogates and CVD incidence
As shown in Table 2, nine IR surrogate indicators-TyG, 
TG/HDL-C, METS-IR, CVAI, LAP, AIP, TyG-BMI, 
TyG-WC, and TyG-WHtR-were analyzed for their asso­
ciations with incident CVD using Cox models. After 
adjustment for covariates (age, gender, residence, mari­
tal status, education level, smoking, drinking, hyperten­
sion, and diabetes), per SD increase in all IR indicators 
was significantly associated with elevated CVD risk. The 
HRs were as follows: 1.09 (95% CI, 1.04–1.14) for TyG; 
1.05 (95% CI, 1.01–1.10) for TG/HDL-C; 1.09 (95% CI, 
1.03–1.14) for METS-IR; 1.13 (95% CI, 1.08–1.19) for 
CVAI; 1.07 (95% CI, 1.03–1.12) for LAP; 1.08 (95% CI, 
1.03–1.13) for AIP; 1.10 (95% CI, 1.05–1.15) for TyG-
BMI; 1.11 (95% CI, 1.06–1.16) for TyG-WC; and 1.11 
(95% CI, 1.05–1.16) for TyG-WHtR. When IR indicators 
were categorized into quartiles, participants in the high­
est quartiles (Q3, Q4) of TyG, TG/HDL-C, CVAI, LAP, 
AIP, and TyG-WC exhibited significantly increased CVD 
risk compared with the reference group (Q1) (P < 0.05). 
In contrast, for METS-IR, TyG-BMI, and TyG-WHtR,

statistically significant risk elevation was observed only in 
the Q4 group (P < 0.05). The dose-response relationships 
between different IR surrogate indicators and incidence 
of CVD were explored using restricted cubic splines 
(Fig. 2). The analyses revealed that TyG, METS-IR, CVAI, 
AIP, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and TyG-WHtR exhibited 
approximately linear relationships with the incidence of 
CVD (all P for Nonlinear > 0.05), whereas TG/HDL-C 
and LAP showed significantly nonlinear relationships (all 
P for Nonlinear < 0.05).
Subgroup analyses stratified by heart disease and stroke 
outcomes were presented in Table 3. Per SD increase in 
all IR surrogate indicators was significantly associated 
with an elevated risk of stroke, whereas only METS-IR, 
CVAI, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and TyG-WHtR were signifi­
cantly associated with an increased risk of CHD (P < 0.05 
for all). When categorized into quartiles, the associations 
between IR indicators and CHD risk were significant only 
in high quantile groups. For stroke outcomes, however, 
all IR indicators demonstrated a progressively elevated 
risk across Q2, Q3, and Q4 groups relative to Q1 (P < 0.05 
for all comparisons).
Predictive performance of nine IR surrogate indicators for 
CVD
This study evaluated the predictive capacity of nine IR 
surrogate measures for CVD onset using time-dependent 
C-index. Figure  3 displays the time-dependent C-index 
for each surrogate measure across follow-up periods. 
The overall C-index was as follows: TyG, 0.742 (95% CI, 
0.737–0.747);TG/HDL-C, 0.739 (95% CI, 0.735–0.744); 
METS-IR, 0.735 (95% CI, 0.732–0.738); CVAI, 0.738 
(95% CI, 0.735–0.742); LAP, 0.740 (95% CI, 0.736–0.745); 
AIP, 0.740 (95% CI, 0.737–0.744); TyG-BMI, 0.736 (95% 
CI, 0.733–0.739); TyG-WC, 0.737 (95% CI, 0.734–0.741); 
and TyG-WHtR, 0.737 (95% CI, 0.733–0.740). The com­
parison of C-indices between different IR surrogates 
was shown in Supplementary Table 2 (Additional file 1). 
Results indicated that the predictive performance of TyG 
for CVD was significantly better than that of the other 
measures.
Discussion
In this large-scale, prospective cohort study of mid­
dle-aged and older Chinese adults, we investigated the 
associations between nine surrogate markers of IR and 
incident CVD, concurrently performing a comparative 
analysis of their predictive capabilities. Our findings 
revealed significant associations between all evaluated 
IR indicators (analyzed as both continuous and categori­
cal variables) and incident CVD. Notably, the TyG index 
exhibited the best predictive performance for CVD risk.
IR was increasingly recognized as a systemic pathologi­
cal driver that extended far beyond the cardiovascular 
system. An expanding body of literature has linked IR to a 
spectrum of non-communicable diseases, including non-
alcoholic fatty liver disease [26], chronic kidney disease 
[27], and multiple malignancies [28]. The latest study [29] 
indicated that the systemic inflammation associated with

remains a subject of debate in the literature. For exam­
ple, two independent studies [35, 36] identified CVAI as 
the superior predictor for CHD incidence and carotid 
atherosclerosis progression, particularly among normal-
weight individuals. Other studies [37, 38] found the 
eGDR exhibited stronger associations with overall CVD 
and stroke risk by analyzing NHANES and CHARLS 
datasets. Xia et al. [39] concluded that TyG-WC and 
TyG-WHtR had better performance in predicting inci­
dent ASCVD. Tang et al. [40] reported TyG’s superior 
performance over TyG-WC and TyG-WHtR in predict­
ing arterial stiffness among overweight/obese individuals, 
while Cui et al. [41] further confirmed TyG’s advantage 
over its modified variants (TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and 
TyG-WHtR) for CVD risk stratification in aging popu­
lations. Given that the results of different IR surrogates 
for CVD risk prediction vary among different studies, 
we compared nine IR indices using a large-scale, nation­
ally representative cohort. Our findings revealed a linear 
relationship between TyG index and CVD incidence, 
and TyG had the best predictive performance among the 
nine IR surrogates. The discrepancies between our find­
ings and previous reports were likely multifactorial. The 
distinct population characteristics including age distribu­
tion, ethnicity, and baseline health status could partially 
explain the differences. Furthermore, another reason for 
the discrepancies might be the different definitions of 
outcomes of interest between studies. In the studies men­
tioned above, the outcomes included CHD, carotid ath­
erosclerosis progression, and a composite ASCVD, while 
the outcome of this study was a composite CVD defined 
by questionnaire. Finally, the differences in the follow-up 
duration might also affect the study results.
Although the precise mechanisms linking IR to CVD 
remain incompletely elucidated, several plausible path­
ways have been proposed [42–45]. First, IR triggers 
compensatory β-cell hypersecretion, leading to hyper­
insulinemia that promotes lipogenesis and contributes 
to obesity, ectopic lipid deposition, and dyslipidemia. 
Progressive β-cell dysfunction eventually culminates 
in hyperglycemia and diabetes mellitus. The sustained 
hyperinsulinemic state additionally activates both the 
sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldo­
sterone system, increasing renal tubular sodium reab­
sorption and blood pressure elevation. Concurrently, it 
induces endothelial dysfunction through reduced nitric

oxide bioavailability and enhanced vasoconstrictor pro­
duction. These pathological processes - dyslipidemia, 
hypertension, and endothelial impairment - collectively 
drive atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease progres­
sion. In the state of IR, increased synthesis of very-low-
density lipoproteins and chylomicrons results in elevated 
serum triglyceride levels. Simultaneously, hepatic IR 
leads to abnormal glucose metabolism, characterized by 
decreased hepatic glycogen synthesis and increased glu­
coneogenesis, thereby promoting higher blood glucose 
levels [46, 47]. This constellation of metabolic derange­
ments may explain the superior performance of the TyG 
index, a composite measure of triglycerides and fast­
ing plasma glucose, in assessing IR. Notably, subgroup 
analysis revealed a stronger association between IR and 
the risk of stroke. This link is likely mediated by elevated 
blood pressure, a critical consequence of IR. Hyperten­
sion is the most prevalent comorbidity among hospital­
ized stroke patients in China (66.6%) [48]. Additionally, 
the heterogeneity of our composite heart disease end­
point, which included a range of cardiac conditions, may 
also have attenuated its overall observed association with 
IR.
Our comprehensive evaluation across nine indices 
underscores the clinical utility of the TyG index for early 
CVD risk prediction in China’s aging population. The 
easy accessibility of TyG makes it particularly valuable in 
primary care settings, especially those with limited access 
to advanced diagnostic tools. In practice, an elevated 
TyG index can serve as an important clinical indicator, 
prompting earlier and more intensive lifestyle modifi­
cations—such as dietary counseling and physical activ­
ity promotion—and guiding the stricter management of 
concurrent cardiometabolic risk factors like hyperten­
sion. However, the clinical application of the TyG index 
is still relatively limited. Future research should focus on 
establishing clinically actionable thresholds for the TyG 
index and evaluating its incremental value when incor­
porated into existing risk prediction models to enhance 
their predictive accuracy.
Strengths and limitations
This study has several notable strengths. First, the utili­
zation of nationally representative longitudinal data from 
the CHARLS database (2011–2020) with a mean follow-
up period of 8.2 years enhances the credibility of our 
findings. Second, the comprehensive comparison of nine 
distinct IR surrogates for CVD prediction provides novel 
insights into risk identification, which holds significant 
implications for early diagnosis and prevention of CVD 
in middle-aged and older adults. Nevertheless, certain 
limitations of this study warrant discussion. Primarily, 
the observational study design cannot establish a causal 
relationship between IR and CVD. Future research, 
potentially employing methodologies such as Mendelian 
randomization, would be valuable to help elucidate the 
causality of these associations. Furthermore, outcome 
assessment was based on self-reported questionnaires, 
introducing the potential for recall bias. To overcome 
this, prospective studies with rigorously adjudicated 
clinical endpoints, verified through medical records or 
registries, are needed to validate our findings. Although 
we adjusted for potential confounders during data analy­
sis, unmeasured confounders might still bias the results. 
Additionally, not all existing IR surrogates were analyzed 
in the study, due to the absence of key biomarkers in the 
CHARLS database, such as fasting insulin levels and vis­
ceral fat area. Future large-scale cohort studies should 
aim to collect a more comprehensive panel of metabolic 
markers to allow for a complete comparison across a 
wider array of IR surrogates. Finally, as our findings are 
based on a cohort of middle-aged and older Chinese 
adults, caution should be exercised when extrapolat­
ing these results to other demographic or ethnic groups. 
Further validation studies in diverse populations are war­
ranted to confirm the generalizability of our conclusions.
Conclusion
This study found that nine insulin resistance surrogates 
were significantly associated with incident CVD among 
Chinese middle-aged and older adults, with the TyG 
index exhibiting the best predictive performance. While 
these findings highlight the TyG index as a valuable tool, 
future studies using objective outcomes in diverse popu­
lations are needed to confirm its broad utility and address 
the limitations of the present study.

Abstract: Background Insulin resistance (IR) is an established independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD). Although numerous simple surrogate indicators for IR have been proposed, their comparative predictive utility for CVD remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the associations between nine IR surrogate indicators and incident CVD and to comparatively assess their predictive capacities using nationally representative data from China. Methods 7,662 participants without CVD from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) were included in the study. Nine IR surrogate measures including triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, triglyceride to high-density lipoprotein ratio (TG/HDL), metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR), Chinese visceral adiposity index (CVAI), lipid accumulation product (LAP), atherogenic index of plasma (AIP), triglyceride glucose-body mass index (TyG-BMI), triglyceride glucose-waist circumference (TyG-WC), and triglyceride glucose-waist-to-height ratio (TyG-WHtR) were calculated. Cox model and restricted cubic spline model were used to estimate the relationships between distinct IR surrogates and incident CVD. We also computed the time-dependent Harrell’s concordance index (C-index) to compare the predictive performance of IR surrogates. Results After a mean follow-up duration of 8.2 years, a total of 1,906 individuals developed CVD. The full adjusted cox model revealed that per SD increase in all IR indicators was significantly associated with elevated CVD risk, with the hazard ratio (95%CI) of 1.09 (1.04–1.14) for TyG; 1.05 (1.01–1.10) for TG/HDL-C; 1.09 (1.03–1.14) for METS-IR; 1.13 (1.08–1.19) for CVAI; 1.07 (1.03–1.12) for LAP; 1.08 (1.03–1.13) for AIP; 1.10 (1.05–1.15) for TyG-BMI; 1.11 (1.06–1.16) for TyG-WC; and 1.11 (1.05–1.16) for TyG-WHtR. Predictive performance analysis showed TyG had the highest C-index of 0.742 (95% CI, 0.737–0.747). Conclusions Among nine IR surrogates, the TyG index exhibited the highest predictive performance for incident CVD in Chinese middle-aged and older adults. Acknowledging limitations such as the observational design and self- reported outcomes, our findings support the TyG index as a simple, powerful, and clinically accessible tool for early CVD risk prediction.
